summary:
B[U]ILT 2 Launch is a pixel-art game that runs in the browser. The player is the Flight Director of a tiny space agency with $800M and a short window to plan a mission. They hire a crew and staff, build a capsule, pick a rocket, launch site, and survive five weeks of surprises. Then they choose a launch day from the weather forecast, hear their team vote Go or No-Go, and watch an animated launch. Every choice changes the odds. When a mission fails, the game shows a real NASA story it resembles, with the NASA source on screen. When it succeeds, players unlock a 3D Earth full of NASA facts.

B[U]ILT 2 Launch takes a whole mission from concept to launch in one game. Players balance budget, mass, power, communications, time and crew, and see how each choice affects the others. A cheaper part saves money but lowers reliability. A rushed test saves days but raises risk. A mission report explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

This matters as most people never see what a full space mission requires. They see a successful launch, but often not the engineering, inspecting, weather forecasting and planning behind it. In B[U]ILT 2 Launch, every step is a job the player takes on. A player can lose a mission, learn from historical NASA experiences, and try again. We hope it sparks curiosity and lets players picture themselves in the field.
details:
B[U]IlT 2 Launch is a browser game where you are the Flight Director of a tiny space agency with $800M and a limited number of days. You play through five stages:

  1. Briefing and hiring. Rosa, a retired Flight Director, welcomes you. You hire 3 astronauts and up to 6 staff.
  2. Build. You choose a capsule shell, life support, power, comms and flight computer. Then you pick a rocket and launch site. A mass check stops a build that is too heavy for the rocket.
  3. The trail. Over five weeks, you assign staff to building, testing and training. A random event hits each week.
  4. Launch week. You read the weather forecast and pick a launch day. Your team votes Go or No-Go, and you can hold, scrub or overrule them.
  5. Launch and report. You watch the four stages of liftoff: liftoff, max-Q, separation and orbit. A mission report scores your run and awards a medal.

How it teaches mission design

Every choice has a cost. A cheap part saves budget but lowers reliability. Skipping a test saves days but raises risk. Power, mass, comms, budget, time and crew all pull against each other, as in a real mission. Launch odds are calculated from all of them. Nothing is simply right or wrong, and the report explains why the mission worked or didn't.

Real NASA stories

Close calls trigger history cards (such as Challenger, Hubble and Apollo 13). Each card shows its NASA source link on screen.

Intended impact

Most people never see the engineers, inspectors, forecasters and planners behind a launch. In Launch Trail they do those jobs. Failure is a lesson, and the player can try again. We want our audience to get curious about the field early, and to see themselves in it.

How we built it

  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules. There are no frameworks, no build step and no runtime dependencies.
  • The game is split into five parts, one per teammate. They plug together through a shared rulebook, a shared game state and a shared UI library. Every screen can run alone on its own test page.
  • A seedable random function makes any run repeatable for testing.
  • We playtested the scoring with about 150,000 simulated games, then rebalanced it.
  • The game is hosted on Azure and deployed automatically from GitHub.
  • All pixel art was hand-drawn in a single 16-color palette. Sound effects were made in jsfxr. The font is Press Start 2P.

What we considered

  • Audience: beginners and youth. Text is short and plain, and a mentor character explains each concept the first time it appears.
  • Replay: try again from the report with a different crew, build or plan.
  • Secret ending: there is a hidden ending for players who find it.

AI use

We used Claude Code to help write code, game text and data files. Use is listed in AI-USE.md in our repo. We used no AI-generated images.
